title: 43 Tests for a Write Warmup State Machine
description:
43 tests. That is what it took to be confident in a state machine that decides whether a posting account can handle more writes today.

The problem: fresh X accounts cannot go from zero to full throughput on day one. The platform watches your write velocity and punishes sudden spikes with code 226 (write limit exceeded). Ignore enough 226s and you get a 14 day penalty stamped on the account. So you need a warmup module that advances cautiously, reads the platform's error signals, and rolls back when things go wrong. A hardcoded delay is not enough. You need a state machine.

The design

warmup.py is built around a single evaluate() function that the publish loop calls before deciding whether to post. Every call checks four gates before advancing to the next phase:

  1. Dwell: enough time has passed in the current phase
  2. No sustained 344s: a sustained stream of "not found" errors means something is broken at the read level
  3. Health: the overall error rate is acceptable
  4. Impression gate: posts are actually landing, not silently failing

All four pass and the phase advances, the write ceiling rises, and the account gets more room. Any one fails and the phase stays put.

The rollback logic

If evaluate() detects a code 226 anywhere in the trailing 7 days, it rolls the phase back by one. That is the first penalty. If the same phase triggers a rollback a second time, evaluate() does not just roll back again: it halts the entire warmup and fires an alert. The account stops posting until a human looks at it.

Why halt on the second rollback rather than keep rolling back indefinitely? One rollback might be noise. Two rollbacks at the same phase is a signal that the ceiling for that phase is genuinely too high for this account. Continuing would oscillate forever and accomplish nothing. Halting forces a decision.

over_ceiling() has three states, which I almost got wrong

False when warmup is disabled (not in effect at all, so ceiling is not a constraint)
True when halted (blocked regardless of write count)
Otherwise, writes_today >= ceiling

The middle case is the one to get right: a halted warmup means over_ceiling() returns True even if writes_today is zero. The publish loop checks this function and must treat True as a hard stop, not a "try again later." Getting that wrong means a halted account silently resumes posting.

WARMUP_PHASES = None in config exists so tests and manual overrides can disable warmup entirely without touching state. Convenient, but it also means the module has a silent off switch that is easy to forget about in production.

The test suite

43 tests cover every public function and the full evaluate() state machine: normal advance, dwell not met, each gate failing independently, first rollback, second rollback at the same phase, halt condition, and reset. Writing the tests before wiring evaluate() into the publish loop forced the edge cases into the open before they could cause a real 14 day penalty on a live account.

What I would do differently

The 7 day trailing window for code 226 detection is a guess. Long enough to catch a real pattern, short enough that one bad day does not follow the account for weeks. I would instrument it in production and likely shorten it to 3 to 5 days once there is real signal.

The halt on second rollback is the most conservative call in the module. There is a legitimate argument for counting total rollbacks across all phases rather than counting per phase. I chose per phase counting because it ties the halt directly to a specific ceiling being repeatedly rejected by the platform. That reasoning is sound on paper. Whether it holds in practice is an empirical question I will answer after the first few weeks of live data.

The startup log line for whether warmup is active does not exist yet. It should. A silent off switch with no log trace is a debugging nightmare.

The state machine itself is not complicated. The 43 tests make sure it stays that way.

title: gookit/gcli v3.5.0 released - easy-to-use, feature-rich Go command line application and tool library
description:
GCli v3.5 Updates: Changes Since v3.3.1

GCli is a command-line application and tool library for Go.
This post covers the main changes from v3.3.1 to the recently released v3.5 (including the v3.4 cycle). These updates focus on developer experience and underlying stability.

If you write CLI tools in Go, a few of these features might be useful. Here are the main changes.

Key Updates

  • Shell completion: Supports zero-registration generation and a dynamic completion mode (bash / zsh / PowerShell).
  • Command middleware: Handle auth, logging, and other cross-cutting concerns via Command.Use() / App.Use().
  • Grouped help: Categorize commands and options into titled sections using Category.
  • Struct binding improvements: Added a field tag rule and support for expanding anonymous nested structs.
  • Interactive input: Automatically prompt for missing values via Question.
  • POSIX short-option merging: Support for -aux splitting into -a -u -x.
  • Robustness fixes: Panic handling, help command behavior, and more.
  • A few breaking changes (migration guide at the end).

1. Shell Completion Improvements

Generating shell completion scripts previously required hardcoding command and option names, meaning adding a new command required regenerating the script. GCli v3.5 improves this workflow.

You no longer need to manually register the genac command. A built-in global option generates the static script directly:

# generate a completion script for your shell, then source it
myapp --gen-completion bash > myapp.bash
source myapp.bash

# zsh / PowerShell also supported
myapp --gen-completion zsh  > _myapp
myapp --gen-completion pwsh > myapp.ps1

Additionally, a dynamic completion mode is now available. The generated script no longer hardcodes names; instead, it calls back into your binary via the built-in --in-completion option to fetch candidates at completion time. New commands will immediately work with Tab-completion without regeneration.

For option values, you can define a list of candidates using Choices:

c.StrOpt2(&format, "format", "output format",
    gflag.WithChoices("json", "yaml", "table"))
// typing `--format <Tab>` now suggests: json  yaml  table

2. Command Middleware

If you need to run auth checks or logging before a command's main logic without duplicating code across commands, you can use middleware.

Handlers registered with Use() run in order before the command's main Func. If a handler returns an error, the chain stops, and the error propagates upward.

// command-level middleware
cmd.Use(func(c *gcli.Command, args []string) error {
    if os.Getenv("TOKEN") == "" {
        return c.NewErrf("missing TOKEN env")
    }
    return nil // return nil to continue the chain
})

// application-level middleware: applies before every command
app.Use(func(c *gcli.Command, args []string) error {
    gcli.Debugf("running command: %s", c.Name)
    return nil
})

Both Command.Use() and App.Use() return the receiver, supporting chaining. Apps without middleware behave exactly as before.

3. Grouped Help

When an app has many commands and options, the help output can become cluttered. You can now group them into titled sections using the Category field.

// group commands
app.Add(&gcli.Command{Name: "migrate", Desc: "run db migrate", Category: "database"})
app.Add(&gcli.Command{Name: "serve",   Desc: "start http server"}) // default group

// group options
cmd.StrVar(&dsn, &gcli.CliOpt{Name: "db-dsn", Desc: "database dsn", Category: "database"})
cmd.StrOpt2(&port, "port", "bind port", gflag.WithCategory("network"))

Groups appear in the order of their first definition, and items within a group are sorted by name. If no category is set, the output format remains the same as in older versions.

4. More Flexible Struct Binding

FromStruct now supports a third tag rule (TagRuleField) and automatically expands anonymous nested structs.

The three available rules, selected via c.FromStruct(ptr, ruleType):

  • gcli.TagRuleNamed (default): flag:"name=int0;shorts=i;required=true;desc=message"
  • gcli.TagRuleSimple: flag:"desc;required;default;shorts"
  • gcli.TagRuleField (new): Uses the field name (SnakeCase) as the option name and reads metadata from independent tag keys. 
type commonOpts struct {
    Verbose bool `flag:"v" desc:"enable verbose output"`
}

type demoOpts struct {
    commonOpts        // anonymous: expands into a --verbose/-v option
    UserName string `flag:"u" desc:"the user name" required:"true"`
    Age      int    `desc:"the user age" default:"18"`
}

c.MustFromStruct(&demoOpts{}, gcli.TagRuleField)
// => options: --user-name/-u (required), --age (default 18), --verbose/-v

The field rule keeps the option name tied to the struct field, while desc, default, and required live in their own tags, making it easier to read and maintain.

5. Declarative Interactive Input

If a required option is missing at runtime, you can now attach a Question. GCli will detect the empty value and prompt the user for input interactively.

c.StrOpt2(&token, "token", "the access token",
    gflag.WithQuestion("Please input your access token: "))

$ myapp deploy
Please input your access token: ▮

If a custom Collector is also set, it takes priority over Question.

6. POSIX Short-Option Merging

GCli now supports merging short flags (e.g., -a -u -x becomes -aux) in a POSIX style. This is disabled by default and can be enabled via Config.EnhanceShort.

c.ParserCfg().EnhanceShort = gcli.EnhanceShortMerge  // 1: -aux => -a -u -x
c.ParserCfg().EnhanceShort = gcli.EnhanceShortAttach // 2: also -Ostdout => -O stdout

It can also be enabled globally:

gcli.SetEnhanceShort(gcli.EnhanceShortMerge)
Level Constant Behavior
0 EnhanceShortNone Off (default), fully compatible with old behavior
1 EnhanceShortMerge Split a group only when all members are bool shorts
2 EnhanceShortAttach Also support value-attached form -Ostdout = -O stdout

A safety check is in place: a group is only split if every character is a boolean short option. Mixed forms like -aO (where O takes a value) are left untouched to prevent misparsing.

7. Robustness Fixes

Alongside new features, several long-standing issues were fixed:

  • Panics are no longer swallowed: gflag.Parser.Parse previously ignored recovered panics. It now returns them as an error for easier upstream handling.
  • help <command> works on the first call: Fixed an issue where it might print unknown input command "help".
  • findSimilarCmd fix: No longer writes a phantom help entry into the registry when an unknown command is run.
  • Command.Copy() fix: No longer clears the source command's hooks due to a shared pointer.

Breaking Changes & Migration

A few internal cleanups require adjustments if you depended on them:

Before After
import ".../gcli/v3/helper" Now internal; inline your own helper
import ".../gcli/v3/gclicom" Removed (unused after cliui migration)
Global --verbose 4 flag Env GCLI_VERBOSE=debug, or gcli.SetVerbose(gcli.VerbDebug) / gcli.SetDebugMode()

The --verbose flag was removed because it bound to a per-app copy that the underlying logger never read, making it ineffective. Use the environment variable or code to control log levels.

Additionally, multiple App instances within the same process now share global options (verbose / help / version / strict / completion).

Upgrade & Examples 

go get -u github.com/gookit/gcli/v3@latest

The _examples/cmd directory in the repository includes runnable examples: struct-flag (field tags + anonymous structs), short-merge (short option merging), and ask-demo (interactive input).

If you run into issues or have suggestions, feel free to open an issue or PR on GitHub. For full API documentation, refer to GoDoc.

Your Pipeline Is 19.7h Behind: Catching Environment Sentiment Leads with Pulsebit

This spike is particularly compelling because it was led by English press articles, which are lagging behind by 19.7 hours compared to Hindi articles. English coverage led by 19.7 hours. Hindi at T+19.7h. Confidence scores: English 0.90, Spanish 0.90, French 0.90 Source: Pulsebit /sentiment_by_lang.

Now, let’s talk about three specific builds you can implement using this newfound pattern:

  1. Language-Specific Alert System: Set a threshold for momentum spikes, say +0.300, specifically for English articles. Use the geo filter to continuously monitor for environmental topics, alerting your team when such spikes occur.

  2. Meta-Sentiment Analysis Framework: Create a routine that feeds clustered narrative strings back through our sentiment endpoint. This will help refine your understanding of how different themes like "women," “environment,” and “activism” are being framed across languages, particularly in emerging narratives.

  3. Forming Theme Tracker: Develop a dashboard that visualizes forming themes such as environmental issues, Google involvement, and waste management. Track these against mainstream narratives ("meet, six, women") to detect discrepancies and emerging trends in real-time.

title: GBase 8a Performance Troubleshooting and Stability Governance: From Slow Queries to Primary-Replica Consistency
description:
Performance and stability issues in a GBase 8a cluster rarely exist in isolation. A query that suddenly slows down, wildly uneven node execution times, unstable results, or even local replica inconsistency can stem from node‑level execution differences, data skew, intermediate result bloat, underlying environment anomalies, or primary‑replica consistency problems. This article integrates node‑level slow‑query diagnosis, data skew detection, intermediate result control, log and audit correlation, and primary‑replica consistency handling into a systematic troubleshooting workflow for your gbase database.

1. Slow Query Diagnosis: Pinpoint the Node First

Before rewriting SQL, determine whether the slowdown is cluster‑wide or isolated to a few nodes. Enable recording of queries that exceed a threshold:

SET GLOBAL gcluster_dql_statistic_threshold = 3000; -- record queries over 3 seconds

Retrieve recently recorded slow queries:

SELECT * FROM gclusterdb.sys_sqls ORDER BY create_time DESC LIMIT 20;

Drill into per‑node execution times for a specific SQL:

SELECT * FROM gclusterdb.sys_sql_elapsepernode WHERE sql_id = 'actual_sql_id';

If only one or two nodes lag significantly while others are fast, investigate that node's resources, data distribution, or local failure. If all nodes are uniformly slow, examine the SQL logic, intermediate result size, or global parameter settings.

2. Uneven Node Load: Suspect Data Skew First

When node execution times differ drastically, data skew is usually the prime suspect. A query like:

SELECT region_code, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM fact_order GROUP BY region_code;

can cause a few nodes to shoulder most of the work if region_code is heavily imbalanced. Diagnosis order: confirm skew → determine if the table's distribution key is flawed or dynamic redistribution is at fault → then decide whether to fix the model, rewrite the SQL, or tune parameters. Parameter tuning alone rarely cures a bad distribution key.

3. Intermediate Result Bloat Can Hurt More Than Scanning

A slow query's bottleneck is often not reading data, but the sheer size of intermediate results. SELECT * quickly inflates result sets, making subsequent sorting, aggregation, and network exchange far heavier. The safer approach is to select only necessary columns, push filters as early as possible, and reduce data volume before large joins. When needed, consult express.log to see which execution stages are truly expensive.

4. Correlate Logs and Audit Trails for Faster Diagnosis

Node‑level statistics tell you which SQL is slow and where, but logs explain why it's slow and what anomalies accompanied it. Focus on express.log (engine exceptions), system.log (crash stack traces), and gcware.log (node state and replica operations). Audit logs reveal the history of bulk operations, DDL changes, and parameter modifications — correlate them with performance dips to quickly narrow the cause.

5. Primary‑Replica Inconsistency: Stop Treating It as a Tuning Problem

When results become unstable, a node behaves abnormally after recovery, or DML succeeds but subsequent reads are inconsistent, shift the investigation to primary‑replica consistency. Common causes include inconsistent local parameters, sudden power loss, RAID controller/driver issues, VM abnormal exit, or manual mistakes. GBase 8a provides the gcluster_suffix_consistency_resolve parameter (default 0; set to 1 to attempt automatic resolution). It can detect and repair row‑count mismatches, schema inconsistencies, and SCN discrepancies, provided the cluster has at least three host nodes.

6. Recommended Troubleshooting Sequence

  1. Is the slowdown global or per‑node? Use node‑level statistics to locate tail nodes.
  2. Is data skew present? Check distribution key design and dynamic redistribution.
  3. Examine intermediate results and resource consumption. Slim down columns and watch execution logs.
  4. Correlate audit and system logs. Look for recent operational anomalies or resource conflicts.
  5. Rule out primary‑replica consistency issues. Prioritise this when instability follows node recovery or environment events.

Layering the investigation before deciding whether to rewrite SQL, tune parameters, scan logs, or repair consistency is far more efficient than jumping to conclusions in a gbase database.

title: What's the difference between Manhattan OMNI and OMS ?
description:
This question came up during a system design discussion with one of my colleagues:

"What's the difference between OMS and Manhattan OMNI?"

At first, I wasn't completely sure myself, so I dug deeper into the topic. Here's the simplified explanation I came up with.

What Is an OMS?

OMS stands for Order Management System.

In industries such as retail, fashion, and e-commerce, businesses need a centralized system to:

  • Track inventory
  • Manage orders
  • Coordinate fulfillment
  • Handle shipments and returns
  • Maintain visibility across warehouses and stores

An OMS acts as the operational brain that manages everything that happens after an order is placed.

What Is Manhattan OMNI?

This is where many people get confused.

OMS is a category of software.

Manhattan OMNI is a specific product that belongs to that category.

Think about it this way:

  • OMS = the concept
  • Manhattan OMNI = one implementation of that concept

Much like:

  • Database = category
  • PostgreSQL = product

or

  • CRM = category
  • Salesforce = product

Why Is It Called "OMNI"?

The word OMNI comes from the concept of omnichannel commerce.

An omnichannel strategy connects all customer touchpoints, including:

  • Physical stores
  • E-commerce websites
  • Mobile applications
  • Customer service channels

The goal is to create a seamless shopping experience regardless of where the customer interacts with the business.

Unlike a traditional multichannel approach, where each channel operates independently, omnichannel commerce keeps everything synchronized.

For example:

  • A customer can buy online
  • Return in-store
  • Check inventory through the mobile app

All while interacting with the same underlying inventory and order systems.

Where Does This Fit in an SFCC Architecture?

Let's follow the lifecycle of a typical order.

Step 1: Customer Places an Order

When a customer clicks Place Order, SFCC handles the commerce side of the transaction.

SFCC will:

  • Validate the cart
  • Calculate taxes
  • Apply promotions and discounts
  • Authorize payment
  • Create the order record
  • Send order details to the OMS

At this point, SFCC's primary responsibility is complete.

The order has been successfully captured.

Now the operational work begins.

Step 2: Manhattan OMNI Takes Over

Once the order reaches Manhattan OMNI, the system must determine how the order will actually be fulfilled.

The first question it asks is:

Where is the inventory available?

Example:

Location Available Inventory
Cairo Warehouse 0
Alexandria Warehouse 2
City Center Store 5

Step 3: Order Routing

Based on available inventory, Manhattan OMNI decides where the order should be fulfilled from.

This process is called Order Routing.

The OMS evaluates factors such as:

  • Inventory availability
  • Distance to the customer
  • Shipping costs
  • Store or warehouse capacity
  • Delivery SLA commitments
  • Business fulfillment rules

For example:

Since the Cairo warehouse has no inventory, Manhattan OMNI may decide:

Fulfill the order from the Alexandria warehouse.

This decision is entirely managed by the OMS.

Step 4: Fulfillment Execution

After selecting the fulfillment location, Manhattan OMNI generates fulfillment tasks.

Examples include:

  • Pick the item
  • Pack the item
  • Print shipping labels
  • Schedule shipment
  • Hand the package to the courier

This is where warehouse operations begin.

Important Distinction

Warehouse employees typically do not interact with SFCC.

Instead, they work with:

  • Manhattan OMNI
  • Warehouse Management Systems (WMS)
  • Barcode scanners
  • Inventory management tools
  • Shipping systems

SFCC focuses on selling.

Manhattan OMNI focuses on fulfilling.

SFCC vs Manhattan OMNI

SFCC Manhattan OMNI
Customer-facing commerce platform Order management platform
Shopping experience Fulfillment experience
Product catalog Inventory orchestration
Cart and checkout Order routing
Promotions and pricing Picking and packing
Payment authorization Shipping and delivery
Order creation Order fulfillment

The Key Takeaway

A common misconception is that SFCC manages the entire order lifecycle.

In reality:

  • SFCC creates and captures the order.
  • Manhattan OMNI determines how the order will be fulfilled.
  • Warehouses and stores execute the fulfillment tasks generated by Manhattan OMNI.

In large enterprise architectures, these responsibilities are intentionally separated.

Commerce is not fulfillment.

SFCC sells the product.

Manhattan OMNI gets the product into the customer's hands.

title: Your Pipeline Is 20.0h Behind: Catching Food Sentiment Leads with Pulsebit
description:
Your Pipeline Is 20.0h Behind: Catching Food Sentiment Leads with Pulsebit

We just discovered a fascinating anomaly: a 24h momentum spike of +1.400 in the food sector. Specifically, this spike was triggered by a single article titled "Firo in Chennai launches a monthly Chef’s Edit." This insight is particularly striking, as it highlights how a localized event can create significant momentum in sentiment, potentially unnoticed by broader models. The leading language for this spike was English, with no lag against the Hindi press, allowing us to dive deeper into how language and location can dominate sentiment detection.

The Problem

If your pipeline isn’t set up to handle multilingual sources and the dominance of specific entities, you might have missed this opportunity by a staggering 20 hours. The leading English article was at the forefront of this sentiment shift, while the rest of the pipeline may have been focusing on more generic or mainstream topics without recognizing the localized momentum. This creates a structural gap that can hinder your ability to capture critical insights in time.


English coverage led by 20.0 hours. Hindi at T+20.0h. Confidence scores: English 0.85, Spanish 0.85, French 0.85 Source: Pulsebit /sentiment_by_lang.

The Code

To catch this spike effectively, let’s implement a simple Python script using our API. We’ll focus on filtering by geographic origin and analyzing the meta-sentiment of the clustered narrative.


Geographic detection output for food. India leads with 12 articles and sentiment +0.25. Source: Pulsebit /news_recent geographic fields.

import requests

# Step 1: Geographic origin filter
url = "https://api.pulsebit.com/v1/sentiment"
params = {
    "topic": "food",
    "lang": "en",  # Filter by English language
    "score": -0.033,
    "confidence": 0.85,
    "momentum": +1.400
}

response = requests.get(url, params=params)
data = response.json()
print(data)

# Step 2: Meta-sentiment moment
meta_narrative = "Clustered by shared themes: firo, chennai, monthly, chef’s, edit."
meta_response = requests.post(url, json={"text": meta_narrative})
meta_data = meta_response.json()
print(meta_data)

In this code snippet, we first filter the sentiment data by the English language related to the topic of food. The API call retrieves sentiment insights that reflect the localized spike. Next, we post the narrative framing back through the sentiment analysis endpoint to score how well the story resonates within its thematic context. This dual approach allows us to capture not only the spike itself but also the surrounding narrative.


Left: Python GET /news_semantic call for 'food'. Right: returned JSON response structure (clusters: 3). Source: Pulsebit /news_semantic.

Three Builds Tonight

  1. Geo-Focused Sentiment Analysis: Create a signal specifically for localized events in food sentiment using the English language filter. Set a threshold of momentum spikes above +1.200 to catch significant trends in smaller markets.

  2. Meta-Sentiment Validation: Implement a scoring mechanism for narratives clustered around entities. Use the meta_narrative string to analyze the thematic resonance of similar stories. This can be critical for understanding how localized events are perceived across different demographics.

  3. Sentiment Monitoring Dashboard: Build a dashboard that tracks the momentum of food-related topics over time, specifically monitoring spikes in sentiment. Integrate the English language filter and cluster analysis to provide real-time insights into emerging food trends, comparing them against mainstream narratives like "firo," "chennai," and "monthly."

Get Started

Dive into our documentation at pulsebit.lojenterprise.com/docs and see how easy it is to implement these insights. You can copy-paste and run the code in under 10 minutes, setting you up to catch the next big spike before it becomes mainstream.

title: SQL Pattern Series #8: The Query Order Pattern
description:
Understanding the order SQL actually processes a query

SQL Pattern Series #8 of 21

A collection of practical SQL patterns that help developers recognize common solutions to recurring database problems.

What You'll Learn

In this article you'll learn:

  • Why SQL does not run strictly from top to bottom
  • The difference between written order and logical processing order
  • Why WHERE filters rows before grouping
  • Why HAVING filters groups after aggregation

SQL queries are usually written like this:

SELECT
    CustomerID,
    COUNT(*) AS OrderCount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY CustomerID
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY OrderCount DESC;

That looks like the order SQL runs in.

But logically, SQL processes the query in a different sequence.

That difference explains a lot of beginner confusion.

The Problem

Many SQL developers first read queries from top to bottom.

That makes sense visually.

The query starts with:

SELECT

So it feels like SELECT must happen first.

But SQL is declarative.

You describe the result you want.

The database decides how to produce it.

Logical processing order helps you understand why certain clauses behave the way they do.

The Query Order Pattern

The Query Order Pattern is the habit of thinking about SQL in logical stages.

A simplified logical order is:

  1. FROM
  2. WHERE
  3. GROUP BY
  4. HAVING
  5. SELECT
  6. ORDER BY

This is not necessarily the physical execution plan.

The optimizer may rearrange operations internally.

But this logical order explains how the query is interpreted.

FROM: Choose the Data Source

SQL first determines where the data comes from.

FROM Orders

This establishes the table or joined result set that the rest of the query will operate on.

Before rows can be filtered, grouped, or selected, SQL needs a source.

WHERE: Filter Rows

Next, WHERE filters individual rows.

WHERE OrderDate >= '2024-01-01'

This happens before grouping.

That means WHERE cannot filter aggregate values like:

COUNT(*)

because those counts do not exist yet.

WHERE works row by row.

GROUP BY: Create Groups

After row filtering, SQL groups the remaining rows.

GROUP BY CustomerID

Rows with the same CustomerID are collected into groups.

Once groups exist, aggregate functions such as:

COUNT(*)
SUM(amount)
AVG(score)

can be calculated.

HAVING: Filter Groups

HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

HAVING COUNT(*) > 5

This is why HAVING can use aggregate expressions.

At this point, SQL has already grouped the rows and calculated the count for each group.

A useful shortcut:

WHERE filters rows.

HAVING filters groups.

SELECT: Choose the Output

After filtering and grouping, SQL determines which expressions appear in the result.

SELECT
    CustomerID,
    COUNT(*) AS OrderCount

This is where output columns and aliases are produced.

That is why aliases created in SELECT are not always available in earlier clauses such as WHERE.

The alias may not exist yet in the logical processing order.

ORDER BY: Sort the Result

Finally, ORDER BY sorts the result set.

ORDER BY OrderCount DESC;

Unlike WHERE, many database systems allow ORDER BY to reference aliases created in SELECT.

By this point, the output result has been formed, so the alias is available for sorting.

Why This Pattern Matters

Understanding query order helps explain many common SQL surprises:

  • Why WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 does not work
  • Why HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 does work
  • Why some aliases are not available in WHERE
  • Why filters before grouping affect the final aggregates
  • Why SQL feels different from procedural programming

Once this pattern clicks, many SQL errors become easier to diagnose.

Written Order vs Logical Order

SQL is written in one order:

SELECT
FROM
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
ORDER BY

But it is logically interpreted in another:

FROM
WHERE
GROUP BY
HAVING
SELECT
ORDER BY

This does not mean the database literally executes every query in that exact sequence.

Modern optimizers are far more sophisticated than that.

But the logical order is still useful because it explains the meaning of the query.

When I Reach for This Pattern

I think about the Query Order Pattern when:

  • a query fails because an alias is not recognized
  • WHERE and HAVING become confusing
  • aggregate filters are involved
  • reports return unexpected totals
  • learners try to read SQL from top to bottom

Examples include:

  • filtering grouped reports
  • calculating counts by customer
  • filtering sales totals
  • debugging aggregate queries
  • explaining why SQL clauses behave differently

Key Takeaway

SQL is written in one order, but understood in stages.

The most useful shortcut is:

WHERE filters rows.

HAVING filters groups.

Once you understand that sequence, many SQL queries become easier to read, debug, and explain.

SQL Pattern Series

This article is part of the SQL Pattern Series, a collection of practical SQL patterns that help developers recognize common problem-solving approaches found in reporting, analytics, and application development.

Previous articles:

  • SQL Pattern Series #1: The Presence Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #2: The Match Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #3: The Missing Data Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #4: The Moving Sum Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #5: The Deduplication Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #6: The Routing Pattern
  • SQL Pattern Series #7: The Running Total Pattern

SQL Bubble Pop

If you are learning SQL or helping others learn SQL, I created SQL Bubble Pop, a mobile game that teaches SQL concepts through quick, interactive challenges and pattern recognition exercises.

The goal is simple:

Learn SQL by recognizing patterns instead of memorizing syntax.

title: Web Developer Travis McCracken on API Gateway Design with Rust and Go
description:
Exploring Backend Development with Rust and Go: A Web Developer’s Perspective

Hey there! I’m Travis McCracken, a passionate Web Developer with a keen focus on backend development. Over the years, I’ve dived deep into various programming languages and frameworks, but two stand out in my journey: Rust and Go. Today, I want to share some insights into how these powerful languages are shaping modern backend systems, along with a few fictional project ideas that highlight their strengths.

Why Backend Development Matters

As web applications grow more complex, having a robust and efficient backend becomes essential. Whether it’s serving APIs, managing data caching, or handling asynchronous tasks, the backend is the backbone that keeps everything running smoothly. Languages like Rust and Go have emerged as go-to choices for building fast, reliable, and scalable backend services.

Rust: The Powerhouse for Performance and Safety

Rust has gained popularity largely because of its emphasis on safety and performance. Its ownership model prevents many common bugs, making it an excellent choice for high-performance API services.

Imagine you’re developing a large-scale API handling sensitive data. Rust’s zero-cost abstractions allow you to write code that is both safe and fast. For instance, I recently conceptualized a project called 'fastjson-api'—a highly efficient JSON API server optimized for speed and security, all built with Rust. While it’s a fake project for now, it demonstrates Rust’s potential to handle JSON serialization/deserialization efficiently without sacrificing safety.

Why Rust?

  • Memory safety without a garbage collector
  • Concurrency without data races
  • High performance suitable for microservices

Go: The Language of Simplicity and Concurrency

On the other hand, Go (or Golang) is renowned for its simplicity and excellent concurrency support. Its minimalistic syntax enables rapid development, especially for building APIs and microservices.

Suppose you are creating a caching layer for your backend. I imagined a project named 'rust-cache-server'—not a real project, but a concept showing how Go's goroutines could handle thousands of cache invalidations per second with ease. The idea is to build an HTTP server that manages cache data efficiently, leveraging Go’s lightweight threads.

Why Go?

  • Easy to learn and maintain
  • Built-in concurrency primitives (goroutines, channels)
  • Fast compilation and deployment

Comparing Rust and Go in a Backend Context

When choosing between Rust and Go, consider the project’s specific needs. Rust may be better suited for CPU-bound tasks requiring maximum safety and performance, such as cryptography or real-time data processing. Meanwhile, Go shines in networked applications, where rapid development and concurrency are priorities.

Here’s a quick rundown:

Feature Rust Go
Performance Excellent Good
Safety High Moderate
Concurrency Managed via async/await and threads Native, lightweight goroutines
Ecosystem Growing with mature libraries Rich, with excellent standard library
Learning curve Steeper Gentle

My Personal Take

Having worked on both sides of the fence, I’ve found that the choice often boils down to project requirements and team expertise. For API-heavy backend systems demanding maximum performance and safety, Rust is a stellar option. Conversely, for rapid development and scalable network services, Go is hard to beat.

In the end, understanding both languages broadens your toolkit as a backend developer. I frequently juggle Rust for performance-critical components and Go for quickly deploying scalable APIs.

Final Thoughts

The future of backend development is exciting, with Rust and Go leading the charge. Both languages address different pain points and open new possibilities for building robust, efficient APIs.

If you’re interested in exploring further, I encourage you to check out my developer profiles for more insights and projects:

  • GitHub
  • Medium
  • Dev.to
  • LinkedIn

Thanks for reading! Whether you’re just beginning or already an experienced backend developer, I hope this peek into Rust and Go inspires you to experiment and see what these languages can do for your next project.

Happy coding!

title: I Build a blog API with Redis - Here's every problem I Hit
description:
I build a blog API with FastAPI + Redis + MySQL.
Three cache problems almost killed my app.
If you also face these problems!
Here's how I fixed each one.

1. Cache Penetration

What's Cache Penetration?

Cache Penetration refers to a scenario where the requested data exists neither in cache nor in the database,causing every request to hit the database directly,thereby increasing the database load.

How to solve?

1.Caching null values

Steps:

  • When a queried key exists in neither the cache nor the database,the result (such as null or an empty value) is cached with a short TTL.
  • This way,subsequent identical requests can be served directly from the cache,avoiding frequent database access.

Example:

...
redis = get_redis()
data = redis.get(cache_key)

# First, check the cache. If the cache entry exists, check whether it is __NULL__
if data is not None:
    if data == "__NULL__":
        return {"data": None, "source": "cache"}
    return {"data": data, "source": "cache"}

# Second, cache miss, query database
value = query_database(cache_key)

# Third, cache the result whether it exists in DB or not
if value is not None:
    redis.setex(cache_key, 60, value)          # cache real data
else:
    redis.setex(cache_key, 10, "__NULL__")     # cache null sentinel (short TTL)

return value

2.Cache breakdown

What's Cache breakdown?

Cache breakdownoccurs when a popular data entry expires in the cache while a massive number of concurrent requests are hitting that same data at the exact same time.All those requests penetrate straight through to the database,putting enormous pressure on it and potentially causing system performance issues.

How to solve?

Lock mechanism:When the cache expires,use a locking mechanism to ensure that only one thread can access the database and update the cache.The other threads wait util the cache is rebuilt before reading the data.

Example:

# Generate a lock key based on the given key
lock_key = f"mutex:{key}"

# Use SETNX operation to acquire the lock. If the key does not exist, set it with an expiration time of 300 seconds.
# This prevents concurrent access.
lock_acquired = redis_client.set(lock_key, "1", nx=True, ex=300)

if lock_acquired:
    try:
        # Successfully acquired the lock, query the database
        value = db_query_func(key)
        if value is not None:
            # Write the result to the cache with an expiration time of 3600 seconds
            redis_client.setex(key, 3600, value)
        return value
    finally:
        # Release the lock
        redis_client.delete(lock_key)
else:
    # Failed to acquire the lock, sleep for 0.1 seconds and then retry
    time.sleep(0.1)
    return get_data_with_mutex(key, redis_client, db_query_func)

3.Cache avalanche

What's cache avalanche?

Cache avalancerefers to a situation where a large amount of cached data expires at the same time or the cache service goes down. As a result, all requests are directly sent to the database, causing a sudden surge in the database's pressure and even leading to its downtime.

How to solve?

Randomized TTL

  • The core idea is to avoid a large number of keys expiring simultaneously.
  • When setting the expiration time for the cache, add a random value.

Example:

import random

expire_time = time + random.randint(0,300)
redis.set(key,value,ex=expire_time)

title: Understanding Async/Await Visually: The Restaurant Analogy Every Developer Remembers
description:
Most developers learn async/await by reading definitions like:

"Async programming allows non-blocking execution of code."

Sounds smart.

But many still can't explain what actually happens.

Let's fix that.

Imagine a Restaurant

You walk into a restaurant.

Synchronous World

A waiter takes your order.

Then stands next to the kitchen.

And waits.

For 20 minutes.

Doing nothing.

Then brings your food.

Then serves the next customer.

Ridiculous, right?

Yet this is exactly how synchronous code behaves.

import time

def make_pizza():
    time.sleep(20)
    return "Pizza Ready"

pizza = make_pizza()
print(pizza)

The program waits.

Nothing else happens.

Async World

Now imagine a smarter waiter.

He takes your order.

Gives it to the kitchen.

Moves to another table.

Takes more orders.

Serves drinks.

Answers questions.

When the pizza is ready, he comes back.

That's async programming.

The waiter doesn't stop working.

The kitchen works independently.

import asyncio

async def make_pizza():
    await asyncio.sleep(20)
    return "Pizza Ready"

Notice the keyword:

await

This means:

"I'm waiting for something. While waiting, let someone else work."

Why Async Exists

Modern applications spend most of their time waiting:

  • Database queries
  • API calls
  • File uploads
  • Payment gateways
  • Email services

The CPU isn't busy.

It's waiting.

Async lets us use that waiting time productively.

Real Example: Fetching User Data

Without async:

user = get_user()
orders = get_orders()
payments = get_payments()

Time:

1 sec + 1 sec + 1 sec = 3 sec

With async:

user, orders, payments = await asyncio.gather(
    get_user(),
    get_orders(),
    get_payments()
)

Time:

max(1,1,1) = 1 sec

Same work.

3x faster.

Common Beginner Mistake

People think async means:

Faster CPU execution.

Wrong.

Async doesn't make calculations faster.

It makes waiting smarter.

Think:

  • CPU work → multiprocessing
  • Waiting work → async

Mental Model

Imagine every function holding a microphone.

Normal function:

"Nobody talks until I'm done."

Async function:

"While I'm waiting, someone else can speak."

That single idea explains 90% of async programming.

Where You'll Use Async

Almost every modern backend framework:

  • FastAPI
  • Starlette
  • Sanic
  • Node.js
  • Deno
  • Modern Django

If your application talks to databases, APIs, queues, or cloud services, async is becoming mandatory knowledge.

Final Takeaway

Async programming is not about speed.

It's about efficiency.

A waiter who serves one table at a time creates a queue.

A waiter who keeps moving creates a business.

Your code works exactly the same way.

title: dbt Docs & Lineage: Self-Serve Documentation for the Modern Stack
description:
dbt docs is the most under-rated leverage point in the entire modern data stack — it is the analytics engineering team's generated answer to "where does this column come from, who owns it, and what runs on top of it?" Vendor catalogs (Atlan, Collibra, Alation) charge five-figure annual fees to produce documentation that ships free out of a dbt docs generate run. The catch is that most teams treat it as a side-effect of CI and never invest in the schema YAML, exposures, source freshness wiring, and hosting story that turns the static HTML into a real internal product.

This guide is the senior data engineer answer to "how do we make dbt lineage the company's data dictionary?" without buying a vendor. It walks through the four artefacts a dbt docs generate command compiles (manifest, catalog, sources, run_results), the difference between OSS model-level lineage and dbt column-level lineage rendered by dbt explorer, the exposures registry as the graph boundary into BI / ML / reverse-ETL, dbt source freshness as a real paging signal, and the auth-proxy + dbt docs hosting patterns that work in 2026. Each section pairs a teaching block with a Solution-Tail interview answer — code, a step-by-step trace, an output table, then a concept-by-concept breakdown of why it works.

When you want hands-on reps immediately after reading, drill the ETL practice library →, rehearse on the SQL practice library →, and sharpen the join axis with the joins practice library →.

On this page

  • Why dbt docs are the platform's marketing site in 2026
  • dbt docs generate — what the static site is
  • Lineage graph — the killer visual
  • Exposures + source freshness — the boundary of the graph
  • Hosting, auth and rollout patterns
  • Cheat sheet — dbt docs and lineage recipes
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Practice on PipeCode

1. Why dbt docs are the platform's marketing site in 2026

Generated, not written — dbt docs is the only piece of documentation that survives a refactor because the build emits it

The one-sentence invariant: dbt docs is generated from the same compile that ships your models, so it cannot drift the way a wiki or Confluence page does — it is the side-effect of a build, not a parallel artefact maintained by hand. Every other property of the dbt documentation surface — column descriptions, lineage, exposures, source freshness — follows from "it is regenerated on every CI merge." Once you internalise "generated, not written," the question shifts from "do we have docs?" to "is the YAML rich enough to be useful?"

Three properties that make generated docs win.

  • Freshness is automatic. The manifest and catalog are recompiled on every dbt build. A new column, a renamed model, a deleted source — they all land in the docs on the next merge. No human curates the diff.
  • Coverage is enforced. Tooling (dbt-checkpoint, pre-commit-dbt, dbt-osmosis) can block a PR if a new model lacks a description, an owner meta key, or column-level docs. Coverage becomes a CI signal, not a manager nag.
  • Lineage is exact. dbt parses every Jinja ref and source at compile time, so the graph is the ground truth. There is no "we think this column comes from raw events" — the graph says it does or doesn't.

The four artefacts every dbt build emits.

  • manifest.json — the parsed project graph. Every model, test, source, exposure, macro is a node. Edges are ref and source calls. The single most important file for downstream tooling.
  • catalog.json — warehouse-side metadata: actual columns, types, row counts. Produced by introspecting the warehouse after dbt docs generate runs the catalog query.
  • sources.json — output of dbt source freshness. One record per source with max_loaded_at timestamp and pass/warn/error verdict.
  • run_results.json — outcome of the most recent run: which models ran, how long, with what status. The basis of CI summary cards and Slack notifications.

The 2026 reality — what changed since 2022.

  • dbt explorer in dbt Cloud now ships column-level lineage out of the box for every Cloud project — no plugin, no OpenLineage wiring. The OSS docs site still tops out at model-level lineage unless you bolt on a third-party parser (sqlglot-based, OpenLineage column-lineage operator, or a paid catalog like Atlan / Castor).
  • dbt Mesh lets multiple dbt projects publish models as public contracts with versioned APIs. Lineage spans project boundaries, so the docs show the full cross-team graph.
  • dbt Semantic Layer (formerly MetricFlow) surfaces metrics as first-class nodes in the docs, with their own lineage back to dimensional models.
  • OSS docs site (dbt docs serve) has been frozen in feature-set since dbt 1.6; new investment from dbt Labs goes into Explorer. Self-hosters can still ship a great experience but should expect to layer column-level lineage on top themselves.

Who owns the data dictionary — the political answer.

  • Analytics engineering owns the schema YAML — descriptions, tests, meta keys, exposures.
  • Data engineering owns the source YAML — sources, freshness SLAs, raw-table contracts.
  • Platform owns the hosting story — where the static site lives, who can see it, how it refreshes, how SSO is wired.
  • Data governance (when it exists) owns the policy — PII tags, retention classes, sensitivity labels — but they live as meta keys in the same YAML, not in a separate tool.

What interviewers listen for.

  • Do you say "docs are generated, not written" in the first sentence? — senior signal.
  • Do you describe the artefacts as "manifest + catalog + sources + run_results" unprompted? — required answer.
  • Do you mention exposures as the boundary into BI / ML / reverse-ETL without being asked? — senior signal.
  • Do you push back on "dbt docs are not a real catalog" with "they replace 80% of an Atlan deployment for free, and the other 20% lives in meta keys"? — senior signal.

Worked example — schema YAML that produces rich docs

Detailed explanation. The single biggest leverage point on dbt docs quality is the schema YAML. A model with no description, no column docs, and no meta keys produces a useless tile in the docs site. A model with full descriptions, owner metadata, PII tags, and doc-block references produces a tile that answers 90% of analyst questions without a Slack thread.

Question. Write the schema YAML for a fct_orders model so that the docs page shows model description, owner, PII flag on the customer email column, a freshness SLA, and reusable doc blocks for the status and currency enums.

Input.

Asset What's missing
models/marts/fct_orders.sql model description, column docs, owner, PII
models/marts/_marts.yml nothing — file does not exist yet
models/docs.md nothing — doc blocks not defined

Code.

# models/marts/_marts.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: |
      One row per completed order in the e-commerce platform.
      Grain: order_id (PK).
      Refreshed hourly from the staging layer.
    meta:
      owner: '@analytics-engineering'
      pii: contains
      freshness_sla_hours: 2
      domain: revenue
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: Surrogate primary key, `md5(order_id || created_at)`.
        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: customer_email
        description: '{{ doc("customer_email") }}'
        meta:
          pii: email
          masking_policy: hash_sha256
      - name: status
        description: '{{ doc("order_status_enum") }}'
        tests:
          - accepted_values:
              values: ['pending','paid','shipped','delivered','cancelled']
      - name: currency
        description: '{{ doc("currency_iso4217") }}'
      - name: gross_amount_usd
        description: USD equivalent of the order subtotal, FX rate from `dim_fx_daily`.

{# models/docs.md — reusable doc blocks #}
{% docs customer_email %}
The customer's email address at the time the order was placed.

**PII class:** restricted. Hashed at the mart layer; raw value lives only in
`raw.shopify.orders` and is masked in non-prod environments via a Snowflake
dynamic data-masking policy.
{% enddocs %}

{% docs order_status_enum %}
The order lifecycle status. One of:

- `pending` — order created, payment not authorised yet
- `paid` — payment captured; ready to fulfil
- `shipped` — fulfilment handed off to the carrier
- `delivered` — carrier confirmed delivery
- `cancelled` — order voided pre-fulfilment

Transitions are unidirectional except `pending → cancelled`.
{% enddocs %}

{% docs currency_iso4217 %}
Order currency as a 3-letter ISO 4217 code (e.g. `USD`, `EUR`, `JPY`).
Conversion to USD happens in `fct_orders` via `dim_fx_daily.rate_to_usd`.
{% enddocs %}

Step-by-step explanation.

  1. The description block under models: is rendered as Markdown on the docs page; the literal block scalar | preserves line breaks and bullet structure.
  2. meta keys are arbitrary user-defined metadata exposed as a JSON object in manifest.json and rendered as a labelled table on the docs page. Common keys: owner, pii, domain, freshness_sla_hours.
  3. Each column gets its own description. For repeated content (PII columns, enum lists, currency codes), call {{ doc("name") }} to inline a doc block from docs.md. The doc block renders inline in the docs page and can be reused across models.
  4. Tests (unique, not_null, accepted_values) also surface on the docs page under each column, alongside their pass/fail history from the latest run.
  5. The combined result is a single docs tile that an analyst can open and answer "what is gross_amount_usd, who owns it, what's the PII story?" without leaving the page.

Owner badge models[].meta.owner
PII badge models[].meta.pii
Column table models[].columns[*].description + types from catalog
Tests panel models[].columns[*].tests + latest run_results
Lineage graph manifest.json edges to/from this model

Rule of thumb. Every model description should answer three questions in two sentences: what is the grain, what is the refresh cadence, what is the source of truth? Every column description should answer two: what does this value mean, what is its allowed range?

Worked example — coverage as a CI signal

Detailed explanation. Generated docs are only useful when the underlying YAML is dense. The way to enforce density is to fail PR builds when a new model lands without a description, an owner, or column docs. pre-commit-dbt and dbt-checkpoint ship CI checks that read the manifest.json and flag the gaps.

Worked example — manifest as a queryable graph

Detailed explanation. manifest.json is just JSON. Anything that can read JSON can query it. Teams that treat manifest.json as a queryable graph build slack bots ("who owns fct_orders?"), backfill PII reports ("list every column with meta.pii: email"), and dependency probes ("what breaks if I drop dim_customers?") without any vendor tool.

Question. Write a Python snippet that reads target/manifest.json and produces a CSV of every column flagged as PII (with its model name and owner). Show why this kind of one-off probe is the cheapest data-governance win in the stack.

Input.

File Contents
target/manifest.json generated by dbt parse or dbt compile

Code.

import json, csv
from pathlib import Path

manifest = json.loads(Path("target/manifest.json").read_text())

rows = []
for node_id, node in manifest["nodes"].items():
    if node["resource_type"] != "model":
        continue
    model_owner = (node.get("meta") or {}).get("owner", "unknown")
    for col_name, col in (node.get("columns") or {}).items():
        col_meta = col.get("meta") or {}
        if "pii" in col_meta:
            rows.append({
                "model":  node["name"],
                "owner":  model_owner,
                "column": col_name,
                "pii":    col_meta["pii"],
                "masking": col_meta.get("masking_policy", ""),
            })

with open("pii_inventory.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["model","owner","column","pii","masking"])
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(rows)

print(f"Wrote {len(rows)} PII columns")

Step-by-step explanation.

  1. manifest.json has a top-level nodes dict keyed by node id (model.project.fct_orders). Each node has resource_type, meta, columns, plus parsed refs and sources lists.
  2. The script filters to resource_type == 'model' to skip tests, sources, exposures. Adapt the filter to also include sources by checking manifest["sources"].
  3. For every column, it inspects column.meta and selects those with a pii key. Combine with the model-level meta.owner to attribute the PII to a team.
  4. The resulting CSV is the input to a quarterly governance review, a Slack bot, or a Compliance dashboard. No vendor licence required.
  5. The same pattern powers Slack bots that answer "who owns this model?" from node.meta.owner and "what depends on this?" from node.depends_on.nodes.

Rule of thumb. Treat manifest.json as your data catalog's API. Every governance question that fits "filter the graph by a meta key" can be answered with 20 lines of Python and no vendor.

Senior interview question on the role of dbt docs

A senior interviewer often opens with: "If your stack already has Atlan / Collibra / Alation, why bother with dbt docs at all? Where does dbt docs win, where does it lose, and what's the right boundary between them?"

Solution Using a generated-vs-curated decision framework 

Decision framework — dbt docs vs vendor catalog
================================================

1. Who maintains it?
   - dbt docs        → generated from CI; analytics engineering writes the YAML once
   - vendor catalog  → curated continuously by a data-governance team

2. What does it cover?
   - dbt docs        → models + sources + exposures + lineage in YOUR dbt project
   - vendor catalog  → everything: dbt models + non-dbt tables + BI tools + S3 lakes

3. What is the lineage depth?
   - dbt docs (OSS)   → model-level
   - dbt Explorer     → column-level (Cloud only)
   - vendor catalog   → column-level across non-dbt sources too

4. What does it cost?
   - dbt docs (OSS)  → $0 + hosting
   - dbt Explorer    → bundled into dbt Cloud
   - vendor catalog  → $50K-$500K/year

5. Where does it land in the org?
   - dbt docs        → engineers own it, no governance overhead
   - vendor catalog  → governance owns it, engineers feed it

Step-by-step trace.

Question dbt docs answer Vendor catalog answer
Q1 maintainer analytics engineering, in YAML data governance team, in UI
Q2 coverage dbt project + exposures everything in the warehouse
Q3 lineage depth model-level OSS, column-level Cloud column-level across all sources
Q4 cost $0 OSS, bundled Cloud five-figure annual fee
Q5 ownership engineers governance

For most mid-size teams, the answer is dbt docs as the day-one default, vendor catalog added later if and when non-dbt sources (S3, Snowflake non-dbt tables, BI metric definitions) cross 30% of the catalog surface.

Output:

Recommendation Reasoning
Start with dbt docs Free, generated, owned by engineers
Add vendor catalog when non-dbt surface > 30%, dedicated governance team in place
Never use both as a wiki the moment two tools claim "source of truth," neither is

Why this works — concept by concept:

  • Generated vs curated — the structural axis — generated docs cannot drift; curated docs always do. Choose generated as the default; add curated only where the dbt graph cannot reach.
  • Coverage vs depth — dbt docs win on depth for everything dbt touches; vendor catalogs win on coverage for everything dbt doesn't touch. The right answer depends on how much of your warehouse is dbt-modelled.
  • Cost is real — a five-figure annual vendor fee buys data-governance bureaucracy. If your team's pain is "where does this column come from?" and the answer lives in dbt, the vendor is overkill.
  • Ownership clarifies — when engineers own the docs (because it's YAML in their repo), updates ship with code reviews. When governance owns it, updates need a meeting. Engineer-owned docs stay fresh.
  • Cost — adoption cost of dbt docs is O(time-to-write-YAML); marginal cost per model is O(seconds). Vendor catalog adoption cost is O(months) plus O($50K+) annually plus O(meetings).

2. dbt docs generate — what the static site is

dbt docs generate compiles four JSON artefacts and a static HTML site — manifest + catalog are the heart, the HTML is just a viewer

The mental model in one line: dbt docs generate runs dbt parse to produce manifest.json, then runs the catalog query against your warehouse to produce catalog.json, then bundles a pre-built static HTML site into target/ — the HTML is just a viewer on top of the JSON, so the JSON is the real product. Once you say that out loud, every dbt docs generate interview question becomes a deduction from "manifest is the graph, catalog is the warehouse metadata, the rest is presentation."

What dbt docs generate actually does, step by step.

  • Step 1 — parse. Reads every .sql and .yml file in models/, seeds/, snapshots/, analyses/, macros/, tests/. Builds an in-memory graph; serialises to target/manifest.json.
  • Step 2 — compile. Renders Jinja in every model, resolving ref() and source() calls into actual table identifiers. The compiled SQL is also serialised into the manifest.
  • Step 3 — catalog query. Runs INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS (or warehouse-specific equivalent) against the target schema. Produces catalog.json with column types, row counts, byte sizes.
  • Step 4 — emit static site. Copies the prebuilt React app from the dbt package into target/, drops the JSON artefacts next to it. dbt docs serve runs a Python http.server over that directory.

What lives in manifest.json.

  • nodes — every model, test, snapshot, seed, analysis. Each node has resource_type, name, unique_id, description, meta, tags, columns, depends_on, refs, sources, compiled_code.
  • sources — every source declared in a sources: YAML block. Each source has freshness config, loaded_at_field, external metadata, column docs.
  • exposures — every exposure (dashboard, ML model, reverse-ETL sync). Each has type, owner, maturity, url, depends_on.
  • metrics — every metric from the Semantic Layer (in projects that use MetricFlow).
  • macros — every macro definition. Most docs sites hide macros by default; you can flip a flag to show them.
  • parent_map, child_map — adjacency lists for graph traversal. The parent_map["model.proj.fct_orders"] returns every node that feeds fct_orders.

What lives in catalog.json.

  • nodes[model.proj.X] — the actual warehouse metadata: column names + types, row count, byte size, last-modified.
  • sources[source.proj.shopify.orders] — warehouse metadata for the source tables.
  • generated_at — timestamp of the catalog query. Use this to know when the docs were last refreshed against the warehouse.

Doc blocks — reusable description templates.

  • Doc blocks live in .md files anywhere under models/. Syntax: {% docs name %} body {% enddocs %}.
  • Referenced from YAML via {{ doc("name") }} inside a description string.
  • Common pattern: one docs.md per domain with all enum lists, all PII notes, all currency / unit definitions reused across models.
  • Markdown rendering supports headings, lists, tables, code blocks, links — anything the docs site's renderer supports.

meta keys — the catalog you build yourself.

  • meta is a free-form dict on every node, source, column, exposure. Use it for owner, domain, pii, retention_days, freshness_sla_hours, slack_channel, runbook_url, cost_center.
  • The docs site renders meta as a key-value table under "Details." Custom tooling reads it from the manifest for governance reports, slack bots, alerting.
  • Convention beats config: pick a meta key naming convention on day one (owner, not owner_name or owning_team) and document it in your engineering handbook.

Common interview probes on the artefacts.

  • "What's the difference between manifest.json and catalog.json?" — manifest is your project graph (compile-time); catalog is the warehouse-side metadata (run-time after introspection).
  • "What does dbt docs generate write to disk?" — target/manifest.json, target/catalog.json, plus the prebuilt HTML/CSS/JS.
  • "Does dbt docs generate need a warehouse connection?" — yes, for the catalog query. The --no-compile flag skips compilation but still queries the warehouse. The --empty-catalog flag (1.6+) skips the warehouse query and emits an empty catalog (useful in PR previews).
  • "How do I inline reusable docs?" — {% docs name %} blocks in .md files referenced via {{ doc("name") }} from YAML.

Worked example — minimal end-to-end docs build

Detailed explanation. The first time a team runs dbt docs generate, the docs site is usually empty of descriptions. The fix is to add one schema YAML and one doc block, then re-run. After two iterations, the docs site is already more useful than 80% of corporate wikis.

Question. Show the minimal sequence — dbt project init, schema YAML for one model, doc block, dbt docs generate, dbt docs serve — and what each step adds to the static site.

# dbt_project.yml
name: 'analytics'
profile: 'analytics'
model-paths: ['models']
target-path: 'target'

docs-paths: ['models']    # tell dbt where doc blocks live

-- models/stg_orders.sql
select
  id::bigint as order_id,
  customer_id,
  status::text as status,
  total_amount,
  created_at
from {{ source('shopify','orders') }}

# models/_stg_orders.yml
version: 2

sources:
  - name: shopify
    description: Replicated from the Shopify Admin API by Fivetran.
    schema: raw_shopify
    loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced
    freshness:
      warn_after:  { count: 2, period: hour }
      error_after: { count: 12, period: hour }
    tables:
      - name: orders
        description: One row per Shopify order, raw payload.

models:
  - name: stg_orders
    description: |
      Lightly typed staging view over `raw_shopify.orders`.
      One row per order; no business logic applied here.
    meta:
      owner: '@analytics-engineering'
      layer: staging
    columns:
      - name: order_id

        tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: status
        description: '{{ doc("order_status_enum") }}'

# Generate + serve locally
dbt deps
dbt parse                  # produces manifest.json (no warehouse needed)
dbt docs generate          # produces manifest.json + catalog.json
dbt docs serve --port 8001 # http://localhost:8001

Step-by-step explanation.

  1. dbt deps installs any package dependencies (e.g. dbt_utils, dbt_expectations). Skip if your packages.yml is empty.
  2. dbt parse walks every .sql and .yml file, resolves ref and source calls, and writes target/manifest.json. No warehouse query happens.
  3. dbt docs generate repeats parse and then runs the catalog query against your warehouse to populate target/catalog.json with actual column types and row counts. Without this step, the docs site shows only what's in the YAML, not what's in the warehouse.
  4. dbt docs serve starts a local http.server over target/ and opens the browser. The index page lists every model; clicking one shows the rendered Markdown description, the columns table (with types from the catalog), tests, and the lineage graph for that node.
  5. The doc block {{ doc("order_status_enum") }} resolves to the Markdown body of the matching {% docs order_status_enum %} block in _docs.md. The body is rendered inline in the column description.

Rule of thumb. The day-one goal is "every model has a one-paragraph description and a meta.owner key." Everything else (column docs, doc blocks, PII tags) is built incrementally as the team learns what analysts ask about.

Worked example — --empty-catalog for PR previews

Detailed explanation. Running dbt docs generate in a PR CI requires a warehouse connection (for the catalog query). On big projects this can take 30+ seconds. The --empty-catalog flag (dbt 1.6+) skips the warehouse query entirely, producing an empty catalog.json. The docs site still renders the graph and YAML descriptions — only column types are blank. Perfect for fast PR previews.

Question. Show a CI job that produces a docs preview on every PR using --empty-catalog, with a comment on the PR linking to the deployed preview.

Worked example — extending the manifest with custom meta

Detailed explanation. The meta dict is the team's homemade catalog. The trick is establishing a controlled vocabulary on day one so every team uses the same keys for the same concepts. A schema for meta is just another YAML — but enforced by CI hooks.

Question. Define a meta controlled vocabulary for the project (owner, domain, pii, retention_days, freshness_sla_hours, slack_channel) and write a CI check that fails when a model uses an unknown meta key or misses a required one.

Input.

Concern Required key Type
Ownership owner string (@team-handle)
Domain domain enum (revenue,product,marketing,finance)
PII pii enum (none,contains,restricted)
Retention retention_days int
Freshness freshness_sla_hours int
Paging slack_channel string (#analytics-oncall)

Code.

# scripts/check_meta_vocab.py
import json, sys
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED_KEYS = {'owner', 'domain', 'pii'}
ALLOWED_KEYS  = REQUIRED_KEYS | {'retention_days','freshness_sla_hours','slack_channel','runbook_url','cost_center'}
ALLOWED_DOMAINS = {'revenue','product','marketing','finance','platform'}
ALLOWED_PII = {'none','contains','restricted'}

manifest = json.loads(Path("target/manifest.json").read_text())
failures = []

for node_id, node in manifest['nodes'].items():
    if node['resource_type'] != 'model':
        continue
    meta = node.get('meta') or {}
    missing = REQUIRED_KEYS - set(meta.keys())
    if missing:
        failures.append(f"{node['name']}: missing meta keys {sorted(missing)}")
    unknown = set(meta.keys()) - ALLOWED_KEYS
    if unknown:
        failures.append(f"{node['name']}: unknown meta keys {sorted(unknown)}")
    if 'domain' in meta and meta['domain'] not in ALLOWED_DOMAINS:
        failures.append(f"{node['name']}: bad domain '{meta['domain']}'")
    if 'pii' in meta and meta['pii'] not in ALLOWED_PII:
        failures.append(f"{node['name']}: bad pii '{meta['pii']}'")

if failures:
    print("\n".join(failures))
    sys.exit(1)
print("meta vocabulary OK")

Step-by-step explanation.

  1. The script reads target/manifest.json (produced by dbt parse in CI) — no warehouse needed.
  2. For each model, it checks: REQUIRED_KEYS are all present, no unknown keys outside ALLOWED_KEYS, enum values are in ALLOWED_DOMAINS / ALLOWED_PII.
  3. Failures are aggregated into a list and printed at the end. sys.exit(1) fails the CI job.
  4. New keys (e.g. cost_center) are added to ALLOWED_KEYS once the team agrees. The PR adding the key is the contract change — visible, reviewed, and easy to audit.
  5. The same script runs as a pre-commit hook locally, so contributors get the error before pushing to CI.

Output (sample failure list).

Failure
fct_orders: missing meta keys ['domain']
dim_customers: unknown meta keys ['team_owner'] (use owner)
stg_clicks: bad domain 'analytics'

Rule of thumb. Build the meta vocabulary as code, not as a wiki page. Wiki pages drift; code that exits 1 in CI does not.

Senior interview question on dbt docs generate

A senior interviewer might ask: "Walk me through exactly what dbt docs generate does. What files does it write, what database queries does it run, and what's the difference between dbt parse, dbt compile, and dbt docs generate?"

Solution Using the four-stage compile pipeline 

dbt docs generate — four-stage pipeline
=======================================

Stage 1 — Parse (no warehouse)
  - Read dbt_project.yml + all .sql/.yml/.md files
  - Resolve ref()/source()/macro() calls
  - Build the project graph in memory
  - Write target/manifest.json
  - Same as `dbt parse`

Stage 2 — Compile (no warehouse)
  - Render every model's Jinja into final SQL
  - Inline the compiled SQL into each node in the manifest
  - Write target/compiled/<project>/<model>.sql
  - Same as `dbt compile` (a superset of parse)

Stage 3 — Catalog query (warehouse needed)
  - For each model + source, query the warehouse INFORMATION_SCHEMA
  - Collect column names, types, row counts, byte sizes
  - Write target/catalog.json

Stage 4 — Emit static site (no warehouse)
  - Copy prebuilt index.html + bundle.js into target/
  - The site reads manifest.json + catalog.json + run_results.json at load time

`dbt docs serve` is independent — just runs http.server over target/

Step-by-step trace.

Stage Command equivalent Warehouse query Output file
1 — Parse dbt parse no manifest.json
2 — Compile dbt compile no compiled/<model>.sql (per model)
3 — Catalog dbt docs generate (no --empty-catalog) yes catalog.json
4 — Static site dbt docs generate always emits no index.html, manifest.json, catalog.json

The split matters in CI: PR previews use Stage 1 + 4 (with --empty-catalog) — fast and offline. Production publish uses all four stages.

Output:

Output file Stage Used by
manifest.json 1 (parse) docs site, tooling, governance scripts
compiled/<model>.sql 2 (compile) debugging, dbt run
catalog.json 3 (catalog) docs site (column types + counts)
index.html + bundle 4 (static) the user-facing docs viewer
run_results.json from dbt run/build docs site shows test pass/fail history

Why this works — concept by concept:

  • Four stages, four concerns — parse is graph construction, compile is SQL rendering, catalog is warehouse metadata, static site is the viewer. Each stage is independent; failures isolate to one stage.
  • Manifest is the API — every downstream tool (docs site, governance scripts, Slack bot, OpenLineage) consumes manifest.json. It is the single source of truth for the project graph.
  • Catalog is optional — the docs site renders without a catalog (column types are blank). Production publishes include it; PR previews can skip it via --empty-catalog for speed.
  • Static site is just a viewer — the HTML/JS bundle never changes per-project. The personalisation is entirely in the JSON. You can self-host the bundle once and swap in new JSON on every merge.
  • Cost — parse is O(nodes + edges); compile is O(models × Jinja size); catalog is O(models × INFORMATION_SCHEMA latency); static site is O(1). The catalog query is the slowest stage on big projects — that's the one to skip in PR CI.

3. Lineage graph — the killer visual

Model-level lineage is free; column-level lineage is the upgrade — both come from the same parsed ref() graph

The mental model in one line: dbt lineage is built from every ref() and source() call dbt's parser encounters — model-level lineage falls out for free in the OSS docs site, and column-level lineage is the next-tier feature in dbt explorer (Cloud) or OpenLineage-style parsers (OSS add-on). Once you internalise "the graph is whatever your Jinja ref() calls say it is," the entire dbt column-level lineage interview surface becomes a deduction from how aggressively you parse the compiled SQL.

Model-level lineage — the default everywhere.

  • Every ref('upstream_model') in compiled SQL is an edge in the project graph. dbt's parser records these in manifest.json under each node's depends_on.nodes list.
  • The OSS docs site renders the graph centred on the node you clicked — upstream parents and downstream children, with click-through navigation.
  • The "Resource Lineage" tab is the second-most-used page on any dbt docs site (behind the model index). It's how analysts answer "if I change this, what breaks?"

Column-level lineage — the upgrade.

  • Column-level lineage requires parsing the compiled SQL to track which input columns flow into which output columns. dbt OSS does not do this; you need either dbt Cloud's Explorer or a third-party parser (sqlglot, OpenLineage column-lineage operator, paid catalogs).
  • The trick is parsing SELECT a, b + c AS x, sum(d) over (partition by e) AS y FROM ref('up') JOIN ref('other') USING (k) and emitting edges: up.a → this.a, up.b → this.x, up.c → this.x, up.d → this.y, up.e → this.y, up.k → this.k, other.k → this.k.
  • Edge cases: SELECT *, lateral joins, CTEs, subqueries, recursive CTEs, window functions, lateral flatten. Robust parsers handle all of them; naive parsers (regex-based) handle none.

The lineage path — source → staging → mart.

  • Sources — raw warehouse tables landed by Fivetran / Stitch / Airbyte / Snowpipe. Declared in sources: YAML, never materialised by dbt itself.
  • Staging models (stg_<source>__<table>) — light typing, renaming, deduplication. One staging model per raw table; one-to-one with sources.
  • Intermediate models (int_<...>) — joins, business logic that isn't shipped to analysts. Often hidden from the docs index via tags: [intermediate].
  • Marts (fct_<...>, dim_<...>) — the analyst-facing layer. Documented heavily, tested heavily, the surface that downstream BI tools query.

Cross-project lineage — dbt Mesh.

  • A dbt Mesh project publishes models as public contracts with versioned schemas. Other projects ref('project_name', 'model_name') to consume them.
  • Lineage in manifest.json spans the project boundary — the upstream model is a "public" node, downstream consumers are in different projects.
  • dbt explorer renders the full cross-project graph; OSS docs render only the current project's slice.

Downstream lineage — exposures + BI.

  • Exposures (next section) extend the lineage graph one hop downstream into BI tools, ML models, reverse-ETL syncs.
  • Some BI tools (LookML, Cube, Lightdash) emit their own column-level lineage to OpenLineage; tools like Atlan stitch dbt's manifest with LookML's lineage into a single graph.
  • For OSS-only setups, declaring exposures with depends_on: [ref('fct_orders')] is the lightweight option — the graph ends at the exposure node, not the BI field.

Common interview probes on lineage.

  • "Where does dbt get the lineage graph from?" — parsed ref() and source() calls in every model's compiled SQL; stored in manifest.json under depends_on.nodes.
  • "What's the difference between model-level and column-level lineage?" — model-level is dbt OSS default; column-level needs an extra SQL parser, available out of the box only in dbt Explorer (Cloud).
  • "How do you extend lineage into BI tools?" — declare exposures; or wire OpenLineage column-lineage parsers; or buy Atlan / Castor.
  • "What is dbt Mesh?" — a way for multiple dbt projects to publish/consume models as versioned public contracts, with cross-project lineage in manifest.json.

Worked example — tracing a downstream LookML field back to raw

Detailed explanation. The most common analyst question on the docs site is "where does this number come from?" The lineage tab answers it for in-project models. For BI fields, you declare an exposure that lists the dependencies — clicking the exposure shows the upstream chain back to the raw source.

  o.order_id,
  o.status,
  o.amount_usd as gross_amount_usd,        -- the column LookML reads
  o.created_at
from {{ ref('int_orders_with_fx') }} o

-- models/intermediate/int_orders_with_fx.sql

  s.order_id,
  s.status,
  s.total_amount * f.rate_to_usd as amount_usd,
  s.created_at
from {{ ref('stg_shopify__orders') }} s
left join {{ ref('dim_fx_daily') }} f

 and f.fx_date  = date(s.created_at)

  status::text,
  total_amount,
  currency,
  created_at
from {{ source('shopify','orders') }}

Step-by-step explanation.

  4. stg_shopify__orders.total_amount maps 1-to-1 to raw_shopify.orders.total_amount via source('shopify','orders'). The graph terminates at the source node.
  5. The full chain in the docs site: looker_revenue_dashboard → fct_orders → int_orders_with_fx → stg_shopify__orders → raw_shopify.orders. Five hops, all rendered automatically once the YAML is in place.
